Fed’s preferred inflation gauge accelerated to 3.8% in October, raising the 2027 stakes for the central bank
body: Inflation moved further away from the Federal Reserve's target in October, reinforcing expectations that another interest rate hike is in cards for December and raising questions about how much more work the central bank will have to do in 2027.

The personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed a seasonally adjusted 3.8% annual inflation rate, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate and nearly twice the central bank's goal.
Excluding food and energy, core PCE was 3.3%, the Commerce Department reported Wednesday. That was 0.1 percentage point above the forecast.
While the Fed officially follows the headline figure, policymakers consider core to be a more reliable longer-term gauge of inflation trends.

A separate report also showed much stronger economic growth for the third quarter, with gross domestic product rising at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate. The strong top-line gain for the economy adds further fuel to the notion that Fed monetary policy is not restricting economic activity.

Consumer spending rose 0.3% for the month, which matched the pace of price increases but was 0.1 percentage point lower than forecast. Income, on the other hand, surged 0.7%, much more than the 0.4% estimate. The personal saving rate rose to 4.1%.

The report comes with the market fully pricing in a quarter percentage point interest rate hike when the Fed meets Dec. 8-9. However, it leaves unanswered how much more rates will need to increase to get inflation back down to the Fed's 2% target. Inflation has been running above target for some 5½ years.

news.title: US October PCE core inflation +0.3% m/m vs +0.3% expected
body: Highlights of the Fed's personal consumption expenditure report for October 2026
There are no big surprises here, though the market could have done without the slightly hot core year-over-year number.

Last month I said we'd need another month to see if inflation was broadening. October doesn't settle that, but it doesn't make the worry go away either. Back-to-back core readings of 0.3% and 0.3% aren't consistent with getting anywhere near 2%. The more interesting part of the report is the consumer. Income beat by a wide margin, but spending fell short and real spending was flat for a second straight month. BEA says government benefits were boosted by one-time Medicare Improvement Fund premium rebates so that's likely the story. Most indications from retailers in reports from the past two weeks suggest that the US consumer is fine, in any case.

Digging into the data core goods inflation was about +0.4% m/m in October, the hottest since February (+0.7%). It was +0.2% in September and around 0.1% in the summer. The three-month annualized pace is about 2.7%, against about 1.6% over six months, so it's speeding up. That's an area the Fed has flagged as a concern.

Other nondurable goods rose 0.9%, its biggest gain since at least January 2025. That alone added about 8bp to core. Notably, 'recreational items' were the biggest driver of that, which is a sector that's particularly tariff-exposted. Magazines and newspapers were somehow also a large contributor, in defiance of a major secular slowdown.

This week, the Fed's Williams tilted more towards forward-looking inflation forecasts and away from the recent dogma of 'we have to get inflation to 2% first'. I suspect that's where the entire debate heads if oil and fuel prices continue to go down. I wouldn't say that with a tonne of confidence though as Warsh has tied himself to getting to target and 3.8% on headline is a long ways away.
I also worry that we're headed into annual price resets in many goods and companies are going to try to push through price hikes rather than eating them.

news.title: US tariff details are better than the worst-case scenario implied yesterday
body: The US is taking another step towards rebuilding the tariff regime that was struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
Yesterday's WSJ report highlighted the potential for broad new tariffs but the details from senior US officials in a Reuters report just out are somewhat better than feared.
Proposed 20% tariff on China, consistent with the existing trade agreement
New tariffs won't stack on top of the 10% and 12.5% forced-labor tariffs
Tariffs capped at 15% for South Korea, Taiwan, EU, Japan, Switzerland
Capped at 18% for Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Bangladesh
Brazil faces additional tariffs under a separate Section 301 investigation, including a proposed 10% tariff on finished aircraft.

The biggest detail here is that the tariffs won't stack. That's effectively a 7.5 percentage point increase for China on goods currently subject to the 12.5% levy, something that was floated as far back as August.
Officials said China would warrant a 40% tariff in the absence of a trade agreement.

None of this should come as a big surprise. USTR Greer telegraphed on Friday that the industrial overcapacity investigation was nearing its conclusion and the administration has long signalled its intention to restore tariffs to previously negotiated levels.

The market has had plenty of time to digest that but there was some risk of a fresh escalation. On the whole, these details should come as a relief for most countries. I'd argue that Brazil is the one that's a problem, and Embraer in particular. Brazilian aircraft have enjoyed an exemption from US tariffs since February 24, when the previous 10% tariff was eliminated.

The US explicitly cited a lack of progress on digital trade and other issues as justification for the additional tariffs and you can't help but think the election results were a big part of this response.

news.title: investingLive European session wrap: Equities and tech selloff deepens, gold threatens $3,500
body: The Monday bounce in risk trades is looking more and more like a fever dream. As the Thanksgiving holiday nears, we're seeing the risk rout return and it's starting to turn into a real beatdown again ahead of the Wall Street open later.

US futures were subdued early on in the day but the selling pressure did not let up all through European morning trade. And that's seeing S&P 500 futures now fall by nearly 2% with the Nasdaq bordering on 3% losses as we await the opening bell. Bring on the pain.

As the risk-off wave hits, we're going back to the same old playbook from last week. The dollar is holding steadier and firmer mostly, with traders also turning to the bond market for some shelter as precious metals crumble once again.

EUR/USD is down 0.2% to 1.0946 with USD/JPY steady at 159.25 on the day. The Swiss franc is an outperformer though, with EUR/CHF falling by 0.8% to 0.9085 on the day. That sees price break the May lows, marking the lowest levels since March.

Meanwhile, 10-year Treasury yields are also down a little over 5 bps to 4.848%. And while lower yields might supposedly be a good thing for tech stocks, the context matters just as much - if not even more. The rush to bonds is essentially a signal that traders are definitely running out of safety options amid a wide selloff in leveraged positions in the likes of stocks, gold, and Bitcoin.
In the commodities space, gold is down 0.8% to $3,525 but briefly broke below $3,500 in the past hour as the downside pressure is building.

All eyes are on Wall Street again and the crucial test for markets will be whether tech stocks can absorb the continued selling pressure at the open or whether we see another wave of liquidation as the session progresses.

And don't forget about the economic calendar too, there's the US PCE price inflation data on the agenda. Another round of inflation fears will do little to help traders and investors grasp at straws in search of a potential turnaround before the Thanksgiving holiday comes around tomorrow.

news.title: Solana's bearish outlook persists amid Fed tightening, prolonged US-Iran stalemate and growth concerns
body: As most other cryptocurrencies, Solana spiked to the upside on Monday after the news of Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO triggered a strong rally in equity markets and helped improve the risk sentiment.
The gains were quickly faded, though, as the Nvidia news didn’t change the bigger picture and the underlying macro headwinds.
Moreover, the WSJ reported yesterday that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and other countries as early as this week.

As a reminder, following the Supreme Court ruling against the reciprocal tariffs, the Trump administration has been attempting to recreate a similar tariff structure through a different legal route, with country-specific investigations providing the justification.

This basically means that the Supreme Court ruling might have temporarily disrupted the tariff agenda without producing a lasting reduction in the effective tariff burden. So, we are going back to broadly similar levels to those imposed in 2025. Overall, this isn't a major gamechanger, but it still adds to inflation and growth concerns.

Keep in mind that the Fed is still expected to raise interest rates, with the extent of further tightening depending on incoming economic data and stock market conditions. Higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions remain a headwind for risk assets, especially cryptocurrencies like Solana, which are particularly sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk sentiment.

Meanwhile, the US-Iran stalemate remains unresolved, with Trump continuing to signal the possibility of renewed military action if negotiations fail. This keeps geopolitical risks elevated and adds another layer of uncertainty.

Therefore, the macro backdrop remains negative for Solana. Looking ahead, Solana will likely remain under pressure. A sustained recovery will likely need a more dovish Fed or a concrete breakthrough in US-Iran negotiations that improves growth expectations and the broader risk appetite.

On the daily chart, we can see that Solana spiked to the upside on Monday but eventually gave back all the gains. If we get a pullback into the major downward trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting the 60.00 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the 98.00 level next.

On the 4 hour chart, we have a minor resistance zone around the 75.00 level. If we get another recovery, we can expect the sellers to step in around the resistance, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to extend the pullback into the major downward trendline.

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor downward trendline defining the bearish momentum on this timeframe. The sellers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting new lows. The buyers, on the other hand, will look for a break higher to pile in for a rally into the resistance next. The red lines define the average daily range for today.
Today we have the US Core PCE price index and the latest US Jobless Claims figures.
